The Convention was called to order at 11 A. M. in the Omega Chapter
House, Bro. Bridgman in the Chair.

was received and referred to the Committee on New Business.

"Chicago, May 14th, 1909
Committee on New Business begs leave to submit the following
report:
moved, that the petition of the Chi Delta Psi Fraternity of
Be it
Toronto University be omitted from the further consideration of this
Convention on the following grounds:
First: Lack of information.
Second: Lack of suflScient support and recommendation by members
within Psi Upsilon Fraternity.

9

Third: The unexpressed but ever present sentiment against crossing
the Canadian border line.

Be it moved, that the Aztec Club of the University of Illinois be
granted a chapter of this Fraternity.
The Committee wishes to go on record as not favoring an expansion
policy. At the sametime, it feels justified in submitting the above
motion. We have only too clearly in mind the remembrance of our
unfortunate experience at Williams.

We are not favoring expansion upon the lines followed by D. K. E.
but we feel that in this instance, the Chapter at the University of
Illinois is not only necessary, for the welfare of our Fraternity, but that
it is necessary immediately.

It must be remembered that a Chapter has been installed since 1902
and thatthis, coupled with the dilatory measures pursued in the present
instance, point most conclusively to the idea that we are not rushing

madly onward in the search for Chapters.
In regard to the Univei-sity of Illinois and the Aztec Club, we have
most certainly gotten all the available facts. We know that the University
is growing in scholarship, in the class of men and in athletics. No one who
has ever visited the University has ever brought back an unfavorable
report of either the University or of the Aztec Club.
The fact that no sinking fund has been provided is not to be wdndered
at, in view of the great amount of money expended during the past few
years by the members of the Aztec Club in their seeking after a Chapter
in this Fraternity.

That the spirit of the Aztec Club is undaunted and undismayed by
the rebuffs which they have already received, is well exemplified in the
trip of Mr. Wilson to Champaign last night. We feel that in the Aztec
Club we have a repetition of the historic Upsilon Kappa.

We firmly believe that the time is coming when the University of
Illinois, through the instrumentality of the Aztec Club, will receive a
charter of this Fraternity. Why not now ? Why not save the money
which is necessarily expended in the working for a Chapter, and invest
it in a homelike and substantial house which will be an asset and an

honor, not only to the University of Illinois, but to the Psi Upsilon
national organization."

Special Resolution No. 1 Resolved, That the following minute be

adopted and that a copy thereof signed by President Bridgman and Recorder
Collings beforwarded to the widow of the late Albert Poole Jacobs (Phi '73):
The Seventy-sixth Annual Convention of the Psi Upsilon

Fraternity in session with the Omega Chapter, Chicago, Illinois,
is desirous of expressing to his widow the deep sense of gratitude
the Fraternity owes to the late Brother Albert Poole Jacobs, of the
Phi Chapter, Class of 1873. By his undying devotion to and tireless
energy in working for the interests of the Fraternity he rendered
in his long, active career services of which it is eminently fitting
that Psi Upsilon should make formal acknowledgment.

warded by telegraph to Brother William Howard Taft,, 5eta'78:

to Psi Upsilon's most distinguished son.

(APPENDIX A)
THE COMMUNICATION OF THE EXECUTIVE COUNCIL TO THE
CONVENTION OF 1909
The New Council. Pursuant to the amendment of Article II, Sec
tion 6, of the Constitution, which became operative in 1908, the last
Convention elected ten members of the Council instead of flve as foi-merly.
The first meeting of the Council was held May 19, 1908. All of the mem
bers elected by the Conventionaccepted their election, except Brother
Robert W. Carle (Beta 1897), who declined. Brother Henry J. Fisher
{Beta 1896), was elected by the Council in his place.
In accordance with the provisions of the Constitution as amended, the
Council divided itself by lot into five classes of two members each, with
the following terms respectively :

Term ending 1909: Brothers Bridgman and Coleman,

Term ending 1910: Brothers Wertheimer and Whiting.

Term ending 1911: Brothers Fox and Shattuck.

Term ending 1912: Brothers Babst and Fisher.

Term ending 1913: Brothers Saxe and Senior.

During the year the officers of the Council have been : President,
Brother Bridgman; Secretary, Brother Coleman; Treasurers, Brother
Senior and Brother Poole. Brother Saxe was elected Recorder of the
Council, Brother Fisher, Archivist, and Brother David Orr (Delta 1897),
was appointed Assistant Secretary.
While the Constitution authorizes the Council to fill its own vacancies,
a resolution was adopted on September 11, 1908, that thereafter the term
of a member elected by the Council to fill a vacancy should be only until
the next Convention, so that the delegates might fill the vacancy for the
full unexpired term. Under this resolution. Brother Austin M. Poole
(Delta 1887), was elected a member of the Council in place of Brother
Senior, resigned, and the Convention will be aske'd to elect this year a
member of the Council for the term expiring 1913, in addition to two mem
bers for the term expiring 1914.
Eleven regular meetings ol the Council have been held during the last
year, with an average attendance of eight members. Printed minutes of
the meetings have been promptly forwarded by the Recorder to the
several Chapters.

New Song Book. Notwithstanding the hope expressed in the last
Annual Communication, the Song Book was not ready for distribution at
the opening of the fall term, although a special committee of the Council
was actively engaged in co-operation with Brother Karl P. Harrington
who had charge of the preparation of the book. The most serious diffi

culty, as theretofore, was found with certain publishers who declined the
use of copyrights. The book was ready for distribution in January, 1909,
and contains the words, though not the music, of Brother Hovey's "Stein
" "
Song and the Rho Owl Song." In accordance with General Resolution
No. 5, of 1908, ten copies of the song book have been forwarded to each
Chapter at the rate of two dollars per volume, and in certain cases, when
otdered, extra copies of the book were sent to the Chapters. In addition
to the books sent to the Chapters, copies have been sold to other members
of the Fraternity and there are now on hand about 150 books for future
sale. It is requested that all Chapters that have not yet paid for their
books will do so as promptly as possible. The thanks of the Fraternity
are due to Brother Harrington, Editor, for his excellent work on the new

book.

The Council deemed it proper to present a copy of the
Song Book to
Mrs. Richard Hovey, widow of Brother Hovey, and to his son, Julian
Hovey, in recognition of the service of Mrs. Hovey in securing the con

Visitation of Chapters. One of the purposes ot enlarging the
membership of the Council was believed to be the more frequent visita
tion of Chapters by members of that body, and the Council has made a

beginning in this direction by sending representatives to the Delta,
Gamma, Lambda, Upsilon, Chi, and Tau Chapters. The practice has been
adopted of sending a copy of the report of the visiting brother to the
Chapter visited after the report has been submitted to the Council at a
regular meeting. It is hoped that another year the number of visitations
may be largely increased.

lease. Brother Fisher, as Archivist, will have general charge of the

Masters of the Rolls. We trust that the Chapters will not become
weary of the frequent reference to the office of Master of the Rolls,
created by the Convention held with Beta Chapter, 1902, but in view of
the fact that only three of the Chapters appear to have complied fully
with the provisions of the resolution as to that oflBce, the Council thinks
it necessary once more to urge each Chapter to appoint the Masters of the
Rolls and to keep up the work originally intended to be performed by
them. It requires patience, perseverance, thoroughness and accuracy, but
the work will b^ appreciated at its full value when the Chapters are

requested to furnish information with respect to their own retired mem

information concerning addresses of various members of the Fraternity.
It is quite impossible for the Council, without considerable expense to the
Fraternity, to keep in touch with eight thousand members, but it ought
to be possible for each Chapter to secure and keep available the addresses
of at least a large percentage of itsown members. Any request to the
Council for information might then be promptly referred to the proper
Chapter for attention. In several instances during the past year Chapters
have afforded such information with very gratifying results.

Treasurer's Report. The report of the Treasurer is submitted

Recommendations. The Council would respectfully recommend:

That a message of greeting from the Convention be sent to the
President, Brother William Howard Taft, Beta '78.

plainly addressed to P. O. Box 1720, New York City, and not to the Psi

address often causes delay in correspondence, and in some instances
communications intended lor the Council have never been received.

Toronto, May 10th, 1909.
Secretary
Psi Upsilon Convention,
Chicago, III.
Dear Sir arid Brother :
The Chi Delta Psi fraternity of the University of Toronto are
petitioning for the ninth consecutive year, to be admitted as a Chapter of
Psi Upsilon. They have never petitioned any other fraternity and they
have made it a fraternity pledge Psi Upsilon or nothing.

I have met the boys and find them a bright, gentlemanly, enthusi
astic body ofstudents; loyal to each other and full of esprit de corps.
Their number comprises head men in scholarship and leaders in athletics.
Their share of the college honors captured by fraternities places them
flrst. As university, the University of Toronto ranks well. The
a

endowment of the University is large and constantly increasing; the
standard of scholarship in every department is being considerably raised.
There are over 2,100 male students. Out of such a large body of men, Psi
Upsilon would have ample material for an excellent choice.
All the leading fraternities are represented here since former petition
ers have been satisfied to go elsewhere for a charter after being refused
by Psi Upsilon.
Canada is a rapidly growing country. The inhabitants are exactly
like their United States brothers in race, language and education. The
political barrier is and should be the only difference between them. If
that barrier is ever to be removed such influences as are engendered
by
Greek letter fraternities would be among the strongest toward bringing
about such a result. These fraternity chapters would in the course of

years become great unifiers of thought and feeling.
Canada is destined to be a great country, in time nearly as populous
as the United States. How much better to face the inevitable and estab
lish a chapter in Toronto now than to wait and weaken the local
standing
of the fraternity here by long delay in representation.

When I was in college, I strongly opposed the establishment of a
chapter in Toronto, but after twelve years of residence in this city I am
convinced that the location as a great American tourist centre, the ulti
mate necessity of including the University of Toronto among our
chapter

85

homes^ the desirability of the class of men availaole for initiation, the
standing and size of the University, the virility of the membership of Chi
Delta Psi who are now
petitioners and the fact that they already have a
fine Chapter House, all make it
very desirable to establish a chapter here,
and as a brother in the bonds of dear old
Psi Upsilon whose welfare is
ever mine from the
heart, I desire to add my petition to theirs.
I trust that the
patience and perseverance of the petitioners in this
case will be favorably considered
by the fraternity in Executive Session
and that a unanimous vote of the
chapters of the fraternity will grant
their admission
amongstus.

Yours in the bonds,
E. S. Dean,
r Chapter,
Class '90,
University of Rochester.

(APPENDIX E3)
Toronto, Canada, 11th May, 1909.

Secretary
Psi Upsilon Convention,
Chicago, HI.
Dear Sir and Brother :
As a Brother in Upsilon, Class 94, and as one who in his undergradu
ate days vigorously opposed what he felt to be an unwise tendency to
extend Psi Upsilon privileges either to the West or the North, I beg to
most heartily endorse this, the ninth application of the local Chi Delta
Psi ol the University df Toronto, for admission to our Fraternity.

I have made Toronto my headquarters for the past eleven years, and
my work has led me into an intimate and appreciative asso/ciation with
the University of Toronto and the men who have made it what it is.

I feel positive in stating that no Chapter has been granted a charter
since my entrance into Psi Upsilon on a basis of better standing iu all
College activities than that shown by Chi Delta Psi to your convention
this year.

The members, most of whom I have met, are strong, sound and pur
poseful, secure in their Fraternity finances and in the ownership of a
commodious home.

There is a still broader view which might apply to this application:
there is necessarily a strong community of ideas and purposes now
developing in the relation of the United States to Canada. Divorcing the
situation entirely from any discussion of annexation, the political, com
mercial and social interests of both countries are rapidly becoming one.

Psi Upsilon, in my belief, should have a Chapter in Canada, should
have it now, and should acquire the strength, resources and
loyalty
embodied and described in the repeated applications of Chi Delta Psi of
the University of Toronto.
Yours in the bonds,
M. R. Jennings,
Upsilon '94.
